items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "diploid"?
options: One of two identical copies of a DNA molecule, joined at the centromere after DNA replication.
The region of a chromosome where the two sister chromatids are held together and where spindle fibres attach (via the kinetochore).
A repetitive, non-coding DNA sequence at the end of a chromosome that protects genes from being lost during replication.
Having two complete sets of chromosomes (2n).
items.answer: Having two complete sets of chromosomes (2n).
items.markingKey: Diploid: having two complete sets of chromosomes (2n).

items.stem: Explain why telomeres are important for cells that divide many times.
items.answer: Each round of replication shortens the DNA; telomeres are lost rather than coding genes; when telomeres are too short the cell stops dividing.
items.markingKey: any 2 from: Each round of replication shortens the DNA; telomeres are lost rather than coding genes; when telomeres are too short the cell stops dividing (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: Explain why the two chromatids of a chromosome are genetically identical.
items.answer: They are formed by semi-conservative replication of one DNA molecule during S phase.
items.markingKey: They are formed by semi-conservative replication of one DNA molecule during S phase [2] [2]

items.stem: The diploid number of humans is 46. Copy and complete the table to show the number of chromosomes, chromatids (where chromosomes have two) and DNA molecules in one cell at: G1, G2, metaphase, and in each daughter nucleus at the end of telophase.
items.answer: G1: 46 chromosomes, 46 DNA molecules (single chromatids). G2: 46 chromosomes, 92 chromatids, 92 DNA molecules. Metaphase: 46 chromosomes, 92 chromatids, 92 DNA. Telophase (each nucleus): 46 chromosomes, 46 DNA molecules.
items.markingKey: one mark per correct stage [4]

items.stem: The diploid number of a garden pea is 14. Copy and complete the table to show the number of chromosomes, chromatids (where chromosomes have two) and DNA molecules in one cell at: G1, G2, metaphase, and in each daughter nucleus at the end of telophase.
items.answer: G1: 14 chromosomes, 14 DNA molecules (single chromatids). G2: 14 chromosomes, 28 chromatids, 28 DNA molecules. Metaphase: 14 chromosomes, 28 chromatids, 28 DNA. Telophase (each nucleus): 14 chromosomes, 14 DNA molecules.

items.stem: A karyotype prepared from a dividing cell of humans in a laboratory in Hanoi shows 46 chromosomes, each made of two chromatids, arranged in 23 homologous pairs. (a) Describe the role of the centromere during mitosis. (b) Explain why telomeres are present at the ends of the chromosomes.
items.answer: (a) Holds sister chromatids together; spindle microtubules attach at the kinetochore; centromere splits in anaphase so chromatids separate. (b) Non-coding repeats lost at each replication instead of genes; protect chromosome ends.
items.markingKey: (a) any 2 from: Holds sister chromatids together; spindle microtubules attach at the kinetochore; centromere splits in anaphase so chromatids separate (1 mark each) [2] (b) Non-coding repeats lost at each replication instead of genes [1]; protect chromosome ends [1] [2]

items.stem: What holds two sister chromatids together?
items.answer: The centromere
items.markingKey: Sister chromatids are joined at the centromere until anaphase.

items.stem: Why are telomeres needed?
options: DNA polymerase cannot copy the very end of a DNA molecule, so some DNA is lost at each replication
items.answer: DNA polymerase cannot copy the very end of a DNA molecule, so some DNA is lost at each replication
items.markingKey: Telomeres are non-coding repeats that are lost instead of genes.

items.stem: Explain the role of histones in a chromosome.
items.answer: DNA is negatively charged and wraps around positive histones forming nucleosomes; this packs the long DNA into a small nucleus and allows condensation.
items.markingKey: DNA is negatively charged and wraps around positive histones forming nucleosomes [1]; this packs the long DNA into a small nucleus and allows condensation [1] [2]

items.stem: In cultured human fibroblasts, telomeres start at about 10,000 base pairs and shorten by about 100 base pairs each division. Cells stop dividing when telomeres reach 5,000 base pairs. (a) Calculate the maximum number of divisions. (b) Explain why cells stop dividing when telomeres become too short.
items.answer: (a) 50 divisions (b) Further replication would lose coding DNA (genes) from the chromosome ends, so the cell stops dividing (senescence).
items.markingKey: (a) (10,000 − 5,000) ÷ 100 = 50 [2] (b) genes would be lost [1]; senescence / stops dividing [1] [4]

items.stem: In cultured human fibroblasts, telomeres start at about 10,000 base pairs and shorten by about 200 base pairs each division. Cells stop dividing when telomeres reach 3,000 base pairs. (a) Calculate the maximum number of divisions. (b) Explain why cells stop dividing when telomeres become too short.
items.answer: (a) 35 divisions (b) Further replication would lose coding DNA (genes) from the chromosome ends, so the cell stops dividing (senescence).
items.markingKey: (a) (10,000 − 3,000) ÷ 200 = 35 [2] (b) genes would be lost [1]; senescence / stops dividing [1] [4]

items.stem: Describe the structure of a chromosome, including the roles of histones, the centromere and telomeres.
items.answer: DNA wound around histones (nucleosomes), coiled into chromatin; condensed in division; two sister chromatids after replication, joined at centromere (kinetochore for spindle); telomeres = repetitive non-coding ends protecting genes during replication.
items.markingKey: DNA + histones [2]; chromatids and centromere [2]; telomeres [2] [6]

(a) State the stage of the cell cycle at which the cells were most likely stopped, and explain why. (b) Calculate the number of DNA molecules in the cell. (c) Explain the meaning of homologous chromosomes.
items.answer: (a) Metaphase: chromosomes are most condensed and visible, each with two chromatids. (b) 96 (c) Same genes at the same loci; one maternal and one paternal; same size and centromere position (may have different alleles).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "a structure of microtubules that attaches to centromeres and separates chromatids during nuclear division"?
items.answer: Spindle

items.stem: Explain why mitosis produces genetically identical daughter cells.
items.answer: DNA is replicated semi-conservatively to give identical sister chromatids; in anaphase one chromatid of each chromosome goes to each pole, so each nucleus gets an identical full set.
items.markingKey: DNA is replicated semi-conservatively to give identical sister chromatids [1]; in anaphase one chromatid of each chromosome goes to each pole [1]; so each nucleus gets an identical full set [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why the cell cycle is controlled by checkpoints.
items.answer: Checkpoints ensure DNA is replicated correctly and chromosomes are attached to the spindle before division, preventing mutations or wrong chromosome numbers being passed on.
items.markingKey: Checkpoints ensure DNA is replicated correctly and chromosomes are attached to the spindle before division [1]; preventing mutations or wrong chromosome numbers being passed on [1] [2]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "cell cycle"?
options: Nuclear division that produces two genetically identical nuclei with the same number of chromosomes as the parent nucleus.
The regular sequence of events between one cell division and the next: interphase, mitosis and cytokinesis.
The stage between divisions (G1, S and G2) when the cell grows, replicates DNA and prepares for division.
The division of the cytoplasm to form two cells after nuclear division.
items.answer: The regular sequence of events between one cell division and the next: interphase, mitosis and cytokinesis.
items.markingKey: Cell cycle: the regular sequence of events between one cell division and the next: interphase, mitosis and cytokinesis.

items.stem: Describe and explain what happens during anaphase.
items.answer: Centromeres split; spindle microtubules shorten pulling sister chromatids (now chromosomes) to opposite poles, centromere first; requires ATP.

items.stem: Explain how a tumour forms.
items.answer: Mutation in genes controlling the cell cycle (proto-oncogenes become oncogenes / tumour suppressor genes inactivated); cell divides repeatedly by mitosis without control; mass of cells forms.

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "carcinogen"?

An unspecialised cell that can divide by mitosis an unlimited number of times and can differentiate into specialised cell types.
A factor or substance that causes cancer, such as tar, UV light or ionising radiation.
The spread of cancer cells from a primary tumour to form secondary tumours elsewhere in the body.
items.answer: A factor or substance that causes cancer, such as tar, UV light or ionising radiation.

items.stem: Doctors in Jakarta are studying patients with lung cancer, which is linked to tar in cigarette smoke. (a) Explain how tar in cigarette smoke can lead to the development of a tumour. (b) Suggest one way the risk of this cancer could be reduced. (c) Explain why cancer is more common in older people.
items.answer: (a) It causes mutations in genes controlling the cell cycle (oncogenes / tumour suppressor genes), leading to uncontrolled mitosis and a mass of cells.
